title: CUT&Tag Data Processing and Analysis Tutorial
author: Ye Zheng
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.bjk2kkye

steps.title: Prepare Environment and Requirements
steps.instruction: Ensure the Linux system has the following software installed: R (>= 3.6) with libraries (dplyr, stringr, ggplot2, viridis, GenomicRanges, chromVAR, DESeq2, ggpubr, corrplot, ChIPseqSpikeInFree), FastQC (>= 0.11.9), Bowtie2 (>= 2.3.4.3), samtools (>= 1.10), bedtools (>= 2.29.1), Picard (>= 2.18.29), SEACR (>= 1.3), and deepTools (>= 2.0).

steps.title: Download Sequencing Data
steps.instruction: Download the FASTQ files from GEO or ENA. Specify the project path (projPath) and use wget to retrieve the R1 and R2 files for each replicate (e.g., H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and IgG).

steps.title: Perform Quality Control (Optional)
steps.instruction: Run FastQC to check the quality of the FASTQ files. Note that discordant sequence content at the beginning of reads is common for CUT&Tag and does not necessarily indicate failure.

substeps.instruction: Download and unzip FastQC v0.11.9 into the tools directory.
Run FastQC on R1 and R2 files, outputting results to the fastqFileQC directory.
Interpret results using the FastQC reference guide.

steps.title: Merge Technical Replicates (Optional)
steps.instruction: If samples were sequenced across multiple lanes, pool the FASTQ files by concatenating R1 and R2 files respectively before alignment.

steps.title: Align Reads to Reference Genome
steps.instruction: Align paired-end reads to the hg38 reference genome using Bowtie2 with specific parameters for inserts 10-700 bp in length.

substeps.instruction: Build the bowtie2 reference genome index if not already present.
Run Bowtie2 with parameters: --end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-mixed --no-discordant --phred33 -I 10 -X 700.

steps.title: Align Reads to Spike-in Genome (Optional)
steps.instruction: Align reads to the E. coli genome (U00096.3) for calibration to normalize epitope abundance.

substeps.instruction: Build the E. coli bowtie2 index.
Run Bowtie2 with parameters: --end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-overlap --no-dovetail --no-mixed --no-discordant --phred33 -I 10 -X 700.

steps.title: Analyze Alignment and Sequencing Depth
steps.instruction: Use R to collect and summarize alignment results and sequencing depth from the Bowtie2 summary files for both hg38 and E. coli.

substeps.instruction: Extract sequencing depth and alignment rates for each sample.
Join hg38 and E. coli alignment summaries.
Visualize results using boxplots for sequencing depth, mapped fragments, and alignment rates.

steps.title: Remove PCR Duplicates (Optional)
steps.instruction: Check and remove duplicates using Picard, particularly for IgG control samples where duplication rates may be higher.

substeps.instruction: Sort SAM files by coordinate using SortSam.
Mark duplicates using MarkDuplicates.
Remove duplicates by setting REMOVE_DUPLICATES=true.
Calculate unique library size and duplication rate in R.

steps.title: Assess Fragment Size Distribution
steps.instruction: Extract fragment lengths from the SAM files using samtools and awk to analyze the size distribution.

substeps.instruction: Extract the 9th column of the SAM file to determine fragment length.
Generate fragment size density (violin) plots and count plots in R.

steps.title: Filter Mapped Reads by Quality (Optional)
steps.instruction: Apply a minimum mapping quality score (MAPQ) filter using samtools to eliminate low-quality alignments.

substeps.instruction: Run 'samtools view -q [minQualityScore]' to filter the SAM file.

steps.title: Convert File Formats
steps.instruction: Convert aligned SAM files into BED format and filter for valid fragments.

substeps.instruction: Filter and keep mapped read pairs as BAM files using samtools.
Convert BAM to BEDPE format using bedtools bamtobed.
Filter for read pairs on the same chromosome with fragment lengths < 1000bp using awk.

steps.title: Assess Replicate Reproducibility
steps.instruction: Calculate the Pearson correlation of log2-transformed read counts across the genome using 500 bp bins.

substeps.instruction: Bin the fragments into 500bp intervals using awk.
Generate a hierarchically clustered correlation matrix in R using corrplot.

steps.title: Perform Spike-in Calibration
steps.instruction: Normalize the primary genome coverage using the E. coli read count as a scaling factor.

substeps.instruction: Calculate the scaling factor S = 10,000 / (fragments_mapped_to_E.coli_genome).
Generate normalized bedGraph files using bedtools genomecov with the calculated scale factor.
Visualize the scaling factor and normalized fragment counts in R.

steps.title: Call Peaks using SEACR
steps.instruction: Use SEACR to identify enriched regions by comparing the normalized bedGraph files of the sample against an IgG control.

substeps.instruction: Run SEACR with the 'non' normalization option (since spike-in was already used) and 'stringent' settings.
Call peaks relative to the control and identify the top 0.01% peaks.

steps.title: Evaluate Peak Quality and Reproducibility
steps.instruction: Analyze the number, width, and reproducibility of the called peaks, and calculate the Fraction of Reads in Peaks (FRiPs).

substeps.instruction: Calculate peak counts and widths in R.
Determine the overlap of peaks between biological replicates.
Calculate FRiPs by overlapping peaks with BAM files to find the fraction of reads within peak regions.

steps.title: Visualize Chromatin Landscapes
steps.instruction: Visualize the data using genome browsers or heatmaps.

substeps.instruction: Load normalized bedGraph files into IGV or UCSC Genome Browser.
Generate heatmaps using deepTools: sort and index BAM files, create bigWig files with bamCoverage, and use computeMatrix and plotHeatmap for gene-centric or peak-centric views.

steps.title: Perform Differential Enrichment Analysis
steps.instruction: Use DESeq2 to identify differentially enriched peaks between conditions.

substeps.instruction: Create a master peak list by merging all peaks and reducing overlaps.
Generate a count matrix of fragments per peak for all samples.
Filter out peaks with low counts (sum <= 5).
Run the DESeq2 pipeline to obtain normalized counts and differential results.

steps.title: Alternative Normalization and Peak Calling (Optional)
steps.instruction: Use alternative tools if spike-in DNA was not used or different peak calling logic is required.

substeps.instruction: Use ChIPseqSpikeInFree for normalization without spike-in DNA.
Use MACS2 for peak calling using the 'callpeak' command with IgG control.

description: Overview of CUT&Tag All dynamic processes that take place on DNA in the eukaryotic nucleus occur in the context of a chromatin landscape that comprises nucleosomes and their modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin-associated complexes. A variety of chromatin features mark sites of activating and silencing transcriptional regulatory elements and chromatin domains that differ between cell types and change during development. The mapping of chromatin features genome-wide has traditionally been performed using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), in which chromatin is cross-linked and solubilized, and an antibody to a protein or modification of interest is used to immunoprecipitate the bound DNA (Fig. 1a). Very little has changed in the way ChIP is most generally performed since it was first described 35 years ago, and remains fraught with signal-to-noise issues and artifacts. An alternative chromatin profiling strategy is enzyme tethering in situ whereby the chromatin protein or modification of interest is targeted by an antibody or fusion protein. Then, the underlying DNA is marked or cleaved, and a succession of enzyme-tethering methods have been introduced over the past two decades. Cleavage Under Targets & Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) is a tethering method that uses a protein-A-Tn5 (pA-Tn5) transposome fusion protein (Fig. 1b). In CUT&Tag, permeabilized cells or nuclei are incubated with antibody to a specified chromatin protein, and then pA-Tn5 loaded with mosaic end adaptors is successively tethered to antibody-bound sites. Activation of the transposome by adding magnesium ions results in the integration of the adaptors into nearby DNA. These are then amplified to generate sequencing libraries. Antibody-tethered Tn5-based methods achieve high sensitivity owing to stringent washing of samples after pA-Tn5 tethering and the high efficiency of adaptor integration. The improved signal-to-noise relative to ChIP-seq translates to an order-of-magnitude reduction
